title: An infrasonic vibration energy harvester using pendulum impact
venue: International Journal of Applied Electromagnetics and Mechanics

sections.heading: An infrasonic vibration energy harvester using pendulum impact
sections.text:
Xiaobin Cui and Junhui $\mathrm { H u } ^ { * }$   
State Key Lab of Mechanics and Control of Mechanical Structures, Nanjing University of Aeronautics   
and Astronautics, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China

Abstract. This paper presents experiments and finite element (FE) analyses of an infrasonic vibration energy harvesting device in which a low-frequency pendulum impacts a cantilever beam type energy harvester. The experiments demonstrate that the energy harvester operates in the frequency range of ${ 2 } { \sim } 8 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and has output power of several microwatts under $_ { 0 . 1 \mathrm { ~ g ~ } }$ excitation acceleration. Moreover, a finite element model with a coupling of impact, vibration, piezoelectricity and circuit is established and used to analyze the output voltage and power. The frequency response characteristics at different pendulum lengths and the distances between the pendulum ball and cantilever beams are measured and calculated, respectively. Useful guidelines for designing the energy harvester are obtained.

Keywords: Infrasonic vibration, energy harvester, pendulum, FEM simulation

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The energy harvester from ambient vibration in the environment, used as a power supply for smallscale electronics, has attracted a lot of attention in the last decade. There are three mechanisms for vibration-based energy harvesting, including electromagnetic [1], electro-static [2] and piezoelectric mechanisms [3–7]. Most harvesters reported in the literatures are linear vibration resonator and operate at several tens of Hertz, or even more than $1 0 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ . However, in some special cases, such as human or wind motions, frequency of the vibration sources is lower than $1 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ in the infrasonic range. The maximum electrical power harvested from ambient vibration depends on the ambient vibration frequencies and drops greatly at low frequencies [8]. To improve output power of the harvesters at low frequency vibration, frequency up-conversion technologies have been presented to harvest lowfrequency vibration energy by amplifying the source vibration frequency. One idea for the frequency up-conversion is to use an impact process to transmit energy. Umeda et al. [9] first proposed an impact frequency up-conversion technology for energy harvesting, in which a steel ball impacts on a piezoelectric membrane and transforms mechanical energy to electric energy. Lee et al. [10] proposed a MEMS type energy harvesting device consisting of a piezoelectric beam with a sharp probe on its tip and a slider with super-elastic NiTi ridges on its surface. When piezoelectric cantilever travels along the ridges, the movement of the slider can cause the cantilever beam vibrating at its high resonant frequency. Kulah and Najafi [11] presented an electromagnetic vibration-to-electrical power generator, which can harvest energy from low-frequency ambient vibrations. The generator converts low-frequency environmental vibrations to a higher frequency by using a magnet, and hence provides more efficient energy conversion at low frequencies. Gu and Livemore [12] demonstrated an impact-driven, frequency up-converting mechanism coupled vibration energy harvesting device, in which a compliant driving beam with a low resonant frequency impacts a high frequency piezoelectric energy harvester, resulting in energy harvesting predominantly at the system’s resonance frequency. Section 2 describes the details of the harvester’s structure. Section 3 describes the finite element model with the coupling of piezoelectricity, circuit, vibration and impact, used to analyze the performance of the energy harvester. Section 4 presents the experimental method and results of piezoelectric harvester. Section 5 gives the experimental and calculated characteristics, and discussion for them.

sections.heading: 2. Structure and principle
sections.text:
The energy harvester consists of a pendulum and two piezoelectric cantilevers. Figure 1 shows the structure of the energy harvester. The pendulum is hanged in the middle of two piezoelectric cantilevers and parallel to them.

The cantilever is made of a lead zirconate titanate (PZT) plate and stainless steel (SS) substrate. A cross-sectional view of the PZT-SS cantilever is shown in Fig. 2. The piezoelectric plate (HAIYING Enterprise Group Co., Ltd) of $1 \ \mathrm { c m }$ (length) $\times \ 1$ cm (width) $\times \ 0 . 2 \ \mathrm { m m }$ (thickness), is bonded at the root of the substrate of $1 0 \ \mathrm { c m }$ (length) $\times \ 1$ cm (width) $\times \ 0 . 5 \ \mathrm { m m }$ (thickness), by conductive epoxy. The unequal lengths of the piezoelectric plate and substrates cause a large displacement at the tip of the cantilevers. The piezoelectric plate is poled along the thick direction and is coated with thin electrodes at the top and bottom surfaces.

![](images/7d20e6d3a92db05fec594d1b78c8f190f6d49c54d49d5dec9a08b655f1370f63.jpg)  
Fig. 2. Cross-sectional view of the composite cantilever.

![](images/09563ecf41c85a40aef596c5342daced6c7ec969049e267b733a3959d76bed17.jpg)  
Fig. 3. (a) FE model of the energy harvester. (b) FE model for the constant excitation between the pendulum ball and cantilever beam.

The pendulum is made of a nylon string and steel ball. The pendulum line’s length is $9 \mathrm { { c m } }$ , the steel ball’s diameter is $1 \mathrm { c m }$ and the gap between the ball and cantilevers is $1 . 0 \mathrm { m m }$ . The property constants and dimensions of the materials in the harvester are listed in Table 1.

As shown in Fig. 1, under an $x$ -directional ambient vibration or impact excitation, the pendulum can xswing and impact the two cantilevers. Through periodical mechanical impact between the pendulum ball and two cantilevers, the energy harvester converts the ambient vibration or impact with low frequency to vibration of the cantilevers with high frequency, and produces electrical output power in the piezoelectric plates due to the direct piezoelectric effect. It is well known that the cantilever with high resonance frequency $\mathrm { > }$ dozens Hertz) usually is not efficient in harvesting the energy of a low frequency infrasonic >vibration. With the employment of a pendulum, which can well absorb the energy of low frequency infrasonic vibration, our energy harvester provides a frequency up-converting vibration energy harvesting means.

sections.heading: 3. Finite element analysis with the coupling of multiple physical processes
sections.text:
The finite element analysis (FEA) software ANSYS is used to build a numerical model with the coupling of piezoelectricity, circuit, vibration and impact for the energy harvester connected directly with a load resistor. Figure 3(a) shows the built numerical model for the prototype described in Section 2.

The 8-node hexahedral coupled-field element SOLID5 is used for the piezoelectric material. The 8-node linear structural element SOLID45 is used for the metal material. The 2-node 3-D string element LINK10 is used for the pendulum line. The CIRCU94 element is a circuit element for using in piezoelectric-circuit analyses and can model resistors, inductors, capacitors, current source, or voltage sources. It is used to model the load resistor to calculate the output voltage or power, and is connected to the electrodes on the piezoelectric plate.

Mechanical impact as a classic mechanical problem has been studied widely [13, 14] and most studies use approximate analytical solutions. Now ANSYS software can model the impact processing by a contact pair. In the model, a surface-to-surface contact pair, in which the impacted cantilever surfaces are defined as target surface and the pendulum ball surface as contact surface, is established and used to simulate the impact between the pendulum ball and cantilevers. In the target and contact surfaces, 3D 8-nodes surface-to-surface contact elements TARGE170 and CONTA174 are employed, respectively. Those elements are applicable to 3-D structural and coupled field analyses.

For surface-to-surface contact elements, the penalty method is chosen to simulate the impact processing. This method uses a contact “spring” to establish a relationship between the two contact surfaces, as shown in Fig. 3(b). The contact pressure is

$$
F _ { n } = K _ { n } X _ { p }
$$

where $F _ { n }$ is the normal contact pressure, $X _ { p }$ is the penetration distance and $K _ { n }$ is the normal contact F X Kstiffness. The tangential force is not been considered by the program. In general, the normal contact stiffness $K _ { n }$ is affected by the bulk modulus of contacted element, element size and the total number of Kdegrees of freedom in the model. In programming, the $K _ { n }$ is calculated by

$$
K _ { n } = F K N * f ( E _ { c } , s i z e )
$$

where the real constant FKN defines a normal contact stiffness factor and is usually from 0.1 to 1.0, with a default of 1.0. In this calculation, FKN is 1.0. $f ( E _ { c } , s i z e )$ is a function of the bulk modulus $E _ { c }$ and the element size [15].

The material properties and geometric parameters of the model are listed in Table 1. The modal analysis result of the cantilever shows that the fundamental resonance frequency is $5 5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , corresponding to bending vibration of the cantilevers. Using the $5 5 \ \mathrm { H z }$ resonance frequency and the capacitance of the piezoelectric plate $( = 7 . 1 \mathrm { n F }$ ), the matched load resistance can be estimated as

$$
R _ { o p t } = { \frac { 1 } { \omega _ { 1 } c _ { p } } }
$$

$R _ { o p t }$ is calculated to be $4 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$

A transient analysis was performed to obtain the output voltage on the load resistor. The Rayleigh damping form [16]

$$
[ C ] = \alpha [ M ] + \beta [ K ]
$$

is introduced into the transient analysis. In Eq. (4), $[ C ]$ is the damping matrix, $[ M ]$ is the elementary mass matrix, and $[ K ]$ Cis the mechanical stiffness matrix. $\alpha$ and $\beta$ Mare the coefficients for the mass and Kstiffness matrices, respective. In the model, $\alpha$ is zero and $\begin{array} { r } { \beta = \frac { 2 \zeta } { w _ { 1 } } = 5 . 8 \mathrm { e } { - 4 } } \end{array}$ [17], where $\zeta$ is the damping αratio for the first mode of the system (about 0.01).

The calculated waveform of the instantaneous output voltage under $_ { 0 . 1 \ \mathrm { g } }$ acceleration at ambient excitation frequency of 4, 5, 6 and $7 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ is shown in Fig. 4. It is found that the impact period is equal to the ambient exciting period, and the output voltage peaks are caused by the impact between the ball and cantilevers. A close-up view of one cycle of the output voltage waveform is shown in Fig. 5. The voltage waveform has two parts. The first part is the low-frequency component which is directly caused by the impact between the pendulum ball and cantilevers. The second part has a higher frequency of $5 5 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , which indicates that the fundamental resonance mode is excited in the cantilevers. Figure 6 shows the calculated normal strain in the Y-direction of the cantilevers under impact. The max strain occurs at the root of the cantilevers.

sections.heading: 4. Experiments and discussion
sections.text:
Figure 7 shows a schematic diagram of the experimental setup. The energy harvester’s dimensions are listed in Table 1, as well as the material property constants. It is attached to an electric shaker and parallel to the gravity. The gap $\Delta$ between the pendulum ball and cantilevers is chosen to ensure that the pendulum ball can impact the cantilever within the frequency range of the interest.

The electric shaker is driven by power amplifier (HED-2A) and a signal generator (Tektronix AFG3022B). An accelerometer (LANCE ULT2056) is attached onto the shaker near the energy harvester to measure the acceleration. The output voltage was measured by oscilloscope (Tektronix TDS2014). The load resistance of the energy harvester is $4 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .

Figure 8 shows measured output voltage waveform of the energy harvester vs. time under an ambient excitation of $0 . 1 \ \mathrm { g }$ acceleration and $5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ frequency. It is seen that the measured voltage waveform is very similar to the calculated one shown in Fig. 4(b). The measured average contact time between the pendulum ball and each cantilever is about 0.015 s, which is quite close to the calculated result of $0 . 0 1 7 s$

Measured frequency of the decaying vibration in the cantilever is about $5 2 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ , which is also very close to the computed one $( = 5 5 \mathrm { { H z } ) }$ ). Thus, the experimental results confirm our calculation method.

Figure 9 plots the measured output power vs. excitation frequency with different pendulum lengths. It is seen that when the pendulum length is shortened from $9 . 5 \mathrm { c m }$ to $6 . 5 \mathrm { c m }$ , the output power increases about $300 \%$ . As the pendulum length is shortened further to $3 . 5 \mathrm { c m }$ , the output power does not increase, but the frequency response range becomes narrower. As the pendulum length decreases, the impact point becomes close to the root of each cantilever, which results in an increase of the contact stiffness $K _ { n }$ . This Kincreases the impact force between the pendulum ball and each cantilever, and the output power from the piezoelectric plates. Figure 10 presents the calculated normalized output power vs. excitation frequency for three different gap thickness under $0 . 2 \ : \mathrm { g }$ excitation acceleration when the pendulum length is $9 . 5 \mathrm { c m }$ . It is seen that the gap thickness affects the maximum output power and frequency response bandwidth. The cutoff angular frequencies in Fig. 10 can be solved from

Also, a proper increase of the distance $\Delta$ between the ball and substrates can increase the impact velocity increases [19], which well explains why the output power increases with the increase of the distance between the ball and substrates.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: An infrasonic vibration energy harvester with a pendulum was presented and investigated to harvester the energy of low-frequency ambient vibration. It is found that the output voltage has two frequency components. One has the same frequency as the pendulum impact, and another the same frequency as the fundamental mode of the cantilevers. It is also found that the output power and frequency band width are affected by the pendulum length and distance between the pendulum ball and cantilevers. Moreover, the finite element model for calculating the coupling of piezoelectricity, circuit, vibration and impact in the energy harvester has been verified by experimental results, and is useful for optimizing the design of the energy harvester.
